transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-27 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Alexei Romanov (CTO, CinderBridge), Priya Shah (ML Engineer), Tom Walters (Infra Lead)

-- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) --
Redwood walked through Optimize console recommendations — prefetc h/ prefix KV cache heuristics, batching policy configs, and a cost-per-1k sessions model. Customer asked about latency SLOs, SOC2, on-prem KMS, and burst scenarios.

Topics: prefix prefetch, cache hit modeling, batch size vs latency, session TTLs, cost sim scenarios, Dedicated vs Hosted routing

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the infra team, and with me is Daniel Ortiz, our SE focusing on runtime and caching. How are you all?
[00:18] Alexei: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see the cost models, we've been thinking prefetch might be big for us.
[00:23] Daniel: Cool. Today's plan: we'll run through three example workloads, show the Optimize console sim, and then dig into prefix/KV prefetch heuristics and how they map to cost numbers. We'll leave time for Q&A at the end.
[00:41] Priya: Perfect. For context we have a chat assistant that keeps a 3k token context, about 200 requests per second at peak, and key sessions last 30-90 minutes typically.
[00:55] Tom: Also infra constraint — our egress budget is tight for 2 of our regions and we'd prefer Private deployment or at least Reserved/Dedicated for production.
[01:05] Maya: Noted. We'll show both Hosted bands and Dedicated cost rows.
[01:12] Daniel: Quick clarification on terminology: by prefix or KV prefetch we mean loading the model KV cache for the initial prompt prefix and common state so subsequent tokens are cheaper and faster. It's different from general output caching.
[01:30] Alexei: Right, so do you precompute per-user prefixes or per-intent? We have many intents but a small set of system prompts.
[01:40] Daniel: Great question. Our recommendation for you based on the heatmap you shared is a hybrid: system prompts prefetch at session start, intent-level prefetch for the top 20 intents, and fall back to on-demand otherwise. That balances storage and hit rate.
[01:58] Priya: How do you model hit rates? Our sessions are bursty — lots of short chats and some long ones.
[02:08] Daniel: In the console sim you'll see we use a simple probabilistic model: hit_rate = alpha * coverage_of_prefetched_items where alpha accounts for drift. For your traffic we suggested conservative alpha=0.7 as a starting point.
[02:26] Maya: I'm going to share my screen — opening the Optimize cost sim spreadsheet in the console.
[02:34] Speaker 1: (screen shared) the spreadsheet has three scenarios: baseline (no prefetch), conservative prefetch, and aggressive prefetch. The rows show per-token GPU ms, per-session prefetch cost, and net cost per 1k sessions.
[02:51] Alexei: I notice prefetch introduces an up-front token cost; can you show where that pays back?
[02:58] Daniel: Yes — look at the "net cost per 1k" column. Example: baseline is $X per 1k sessions (higher per-token runtime since you can't reuse KV), conservative prefetch reduces per-request decode time by ~18% giving net saving when average session length > 12 tokens after prefix. Aggressive prefetch has larger frontload but higher hit rate so bigger savings at high repeat rates.
[03:26] Priya: Is there math for cache eviction? Our sessions rotate — after 2 hours entries get evicted currently.
[03:34] Daniel: TTL is configurable. Typical recommendation: session TTL = median session idle + 10%, so for you with 30–90 minute sessions we suggested 100–120 minutes to capture most reuse without blowing memory.
[03:48] Tom: And memory footprint per prefetched entry? We need numbers to size Dedicated pools.
[03:54] Daniel: Per-entry depends on model and quantization. For our 7B float16 model a prefix snapshot is ~120MB; quantized INT8 drops to ~38MB. The console shows per-model footprint rows.
[04:10] Alexei: That's a big delta — do you recommend quantized prefetch always?
[04:15] Daniel: For most web chat workloads yes, INT8 gives good perf/cost for KV without degrading token quality materially. But if you have highly sensitive generation quality for certain flows we can keep FP16 for those specific intents and quantize the rest.
[04:33] Priya: How about batching? We need to maintain <250ms p95 for interactive flows.
[04:40] Daniel: Batching increases throughput but adds latency. The Optimize console runs latency-aware batching sims: with your QPS pattern, continuous batching with max batch size 16 and max wait 10ms keeps median low and p95 around 230ms for most requests. If you need stricter p95 you reduce max batch size or enable priority routing for interactive paths.
[05:03] Maya: I'll toggle to the "latency budget" mode in the sim to show tradeoffs.
[05:09] Speaker 1: (clicks) latency budget set to 250ms p95 — simulator recomputes batching and prefetch savings.
[05:16] Daniel: Note: caching and batching are complementary. Prefetch reduces per-token compute which compresses token processing time; that makes batching more effective because you can pack more within the same latency envelope.
[05:33] Alexei: If we move to Dedicated would we still use the same prefetch logic? Or does Dedicated change the economics?
[05:42] Daniel: Dedicated changes the per-hour compute costs and gives consistent throughput so prefetch ROI is slightly lower on Dedicated if you have low variability. But for you, where egress limits push you to reduce per-token usage, prefetch still has material benefits. The sim shows Dedicated vs Hosted rows so you can compare.
[06:01] Priya: Any considerations for cold-start bursts? We have periodic marketing campaigns that spike sessions 10x for 15 minutes.
[06:09] Daniel: Two tactics: 1) warmup pool (reserve some Dedicated capacity to absorb short spikes) and 2) opportunistic prefetch for sessions arriving in the spike using a higher alpha threshold for likely intents. Also the console can model burst fallback: when capacity is constrained, route to smaller model variants or fall back to hosted non-dedicated with throttled concurrency.
[06:34] Tom: For compliance we need KMS and audit logs if we go Private. Is that baked into the Private package?
[06:41] Maya: Yes. Private supports customer-managed KMS + HSM integration and we provide audit logs, SSO/SAML integrations, RBAC. I'll attach the checklist.
[06:52] Alexei: How does data residency factor in if we have EU customers?
[06:57] Daniel: You can deploy Private in your VPC in the region, or we can ensure Dedicated capacity is in an EU region. The console shows regionized cost columns.
[07:09] Priya: Can you show a concrete CSV output from the sim? Something we can plug into our finance model.
[07:16] Daniel: Sure — exporting... (pause) sending link in chat: https://redwood.example/sim-export/ff-20260227-cinderbridge.csv — note: placeholder link.
[07:32] Alexei: Perfect, we'll use that.
[07:35] Maya: Quick pivot — on quality regressions, Optimize supports regression alerts tied to prompt test sets. You can pin a model version and if prefetch+quantization changes quality we alert.
[07:49] Priya: Good, quality guardrails are a must.
[07:53] Speaker 1: (longer section) Daniel walked through a sample cost sim calculation: assume 1k sessions, median session length 45 tokens post-prefix, prefix 150 tokens, prefetch hit rate 0.6 (conservative), token cost baseline $0.0025 per 1k tokens, compute savings due to KV reuse 20% on decode, net saving X%. There was some mumbled math, occasional mis-said numbers, and a small correction by Daniel at [09:30].
[09:18] Daniel: Sorry small correction — earlier I said 20% decode saving, that was for model variant A; for variant B it's closer to 14%. I'll update the export.
[09:30] Alexei: Are you able to run an on-prem benchmark for our model binary? We run a custom LoRA fine-tuned model.
[09:39] Daniel: Yes, our sandbox supports customer model kernels; we can ingest your artifact and run a 4-hour pilot to measure KV snapshot size and real hit rates. That would be part of the pilot.
[09:51] Priya: What's the expected turnaround?
[09:55] Daniel: Once we get artifacts and access, 3 business days to kick off the pilot and then results within 48 hours of the run.
[10:02] Tom: Networking question — if we do Private VPC, what are the egress patterns for updates/telemetry? We need minimal outbound to meet our firewall rules.
[10:11] Maya: Private can be air-gapped for updates if needed; telemetry can be shipped via a customer-provisioned egress proxy or via a signed S3 export. We'll include details in the checklist.
[10:23] Alexei: Any gotchas for session affinity? We want a user's session to hit the same GPU for latency reasons.
[10:31] Daniel: Session affinity is supported. We use a sticky key routing so a client's session ID maps to an active worker; that increases cache locality but reduces global batching efficiency a bit. The sim includes a "session_affinity" toggle to show cost changes.
[10:46] Priya: Could you quantify the tradeoff? If we enable affinity how much does batching efficiency drop?
[10:52] Daniel: In our tests for similar traffic patterns, batching efficiency dropped ~8–12% but cache hit rates increased 15–20% — net depends on your session lengths. For CinderBridge it's likely net positive because of long sessions.
[11:09] Alexei: On quantization, any impact on hallucination/quality we should measure?
[11:15] Daniel: We recommend running your prompt set through both FP16 and INT8 within pilot. For most retrieval/assistant flows INT8 is within noise, but for very sensitive summarization we saw slight variance. Optimize will tie QA metrics to prompt sets so you can detect regressions.
[11:33] Maya: We're at the halfway mark; any specific numbers you want us to include in the simulation export?
[11:38] Alexei: Please include per-region cost, prefetch hit assumptions, TTL settings, quantization footprint, and a conservative ROI column.
[11:46] Daniel: Will do. Also, one practical recommendation: start with conservative prefetch for system prompts and top intents, TTL 100 minutes, quantized KV, and a batch size cap of 12. Then run pilot to tune aggressive prefetch for high-repeat intents.
[12:03] Priya: That sounds reasonable. One more question: how do you handle TTL eviction when disk is used versus in-memory?
[12:11] Daniel: We tier KV snapshots: hot in-memory for the most active sessions; warm on fast NVMe and cold on object storage. Eviction policy is LRU with pinning for critical flows. The pricing model in the sim accounts for the different storage tiers.
[12:27] Tom: Storage pricing — is NVMe charged per-GB-hour in Dedicated?
[12:32] Daniel: Yes NVMe is charged hourly; the sim maps it to per-session amortized cost based on footprint and TTL.
[12:40] Alexei: Can you show an example where prefetch is not worth it?
[12:45] Daniel: Sure — low-repeat stateless requests with median session length <8 tokens post-prefix. In that case the prefetch frontload never pays back. Also if your QPS is extremely low and you have no repeated intents, it won't be beneficial.
[13:02] Priya: Our marketing spike — would aggressive prefetch help there?
[13:06] Daniel: Only if the spike contains repeated intents; otherwise it hurts. For spikes consider warm pools plus fallback to smaller models.
[13:15] Alexei: Competitor question — how is this different from Anthropic or OpenAI offering?
[13:20] Maya: Our differentiation is the runtime-level support for prefix KV snapshots, console-driven sims tailored to your traffic, and the Unified deployment modes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) with consistent tooling. We also provide regression alerts tied to your prompt sets.
[13:36] Tom: Any risks if we push aggressive prefetch on a fine-tuned LoRA?
[13:41] Daniel: Main risk is unexpected model memory footprint variance; pilot will measure that. Also need to validate that quantization preserves your fine-tune behavior.
[13:52] Priya: Let's talk about instrumentation — what telemetry do you capture to validate hit rates?
[13:58] Daniel: We capture per-session prefetch attempts, cache hit/miss events, KV load times, per-token latencies, and per-tenant cost aggregation. That data is available in the Console with token-level breakdowns.
[14:14] Alexei: Great. On the cost sim CSV you sent, there's a column labeled "token-ms" — can you explain?
[14:20] Daniel: That's an internal metric approximating GPU-ms per token; it's used to normalize across hardware types. The console translates it into $ using the selected kernel/hardware profile.
[14:31] Maya: We're getting some chat here in the meeting — sending SOC2 link and the Private checklist now.
[14:36] Speaker 1: (link posted) https://redwood.example/security/soc2-summary.pdf (placeholder)
[14:42] Alexei: Thanks. A few tangents — curious about multi-region replication of KV snapshots for lower latency in EU.
[14:49] Daniel: We support active-active region routing with KV replication; cost increases due to double storage and sync overhead, but p95 improves. The console can simulate multi-region replication buckets.
[15:05] Priya: If we do replication, how do you handle eventual consistency for prefix state?
[15:11] Daniel: We use last-write-wins for non-critical metadata and pin essential sequences during prefetch. There's a small window for divergence but it's acceptable for most assistant flows. We'll detail constraints in the pilot doc.
[15:26] Tom: Any network encryption requirements between your control plane and Private nodes?
[15:31] Maya: All control plane comms are via mTLS and we support customer-managed VPN tunnels.
[15:36] Alexei: Can you email the sample pilot plan and estimated costs for 1 month of Dedicated capacity with our traffic profile?
[15:43] Maya: Yes — that's part of the next steps.
[15:46] 
[15:48] -- Rapid Q&A and clarifying numbers, a few sections with crosstalk and quick math corrections --
[26:00] Daniel: (deep dive) Here's the per-1k session numbers: baseline $1,260, conservative prefetch $1,040, aggressive $890 — these are illustrative and depend on live hit rates.
[26:16] Alexei: Ok that delta is interesting. If we extrapolate to 1M sessions per month that's meaningful.
[26:24] Priya: Please annotate the CSV with the assumptions used for each row so finance can trace it.
[26:31] Daniel: Will do.
[26:34] Alexei: One more enterprise concern — how do you handle audit logs and forensics if a session is flagged?
[26:41] Maya: We write per-request logs with redaction filters; logs can be stored in your S3 or in a customer-managed logging cluster. We'll share retention policy options.
[26:52] Tom: Could you give an example of fallback routing policy for overload?
[26:57] Daniel: Example policy: if 95th latency > 1s or queue depth > threshold, route new sessions to lower-cost model variant, stream partial responses, and mark requests with "fallback" tag so you can reconcile quality.
[27:12] Alexei: Nice.
[27:15] Priya: Shall we talk pilot scope now? We need to define success criteria.
[27:20] Maya: Suggested success metrics: 10–15% net cost reduction vs baseline, p95 remains under 300ms, no more than 1% quality regression on the prompt devset, and stable KV memory footprint within the Dedicated pool.
[27:35] Alexei: Agreed. Let's also include an operational metric: ability to absorb 10x spike for 15 minutes with <5% error rate.
[27:45] Daniel: Good add.
[27:47] Maya: I'll capture that.
[27:50] Alexei: Who's the contact for billing questions?
[27:53] Maya: That's me — I'll loop in our pricing team for detailed bands.
[27:58] 
[28:00] -- Final recap --
[28:02] Maya: To recap: Redwood will (1) send detailed CSV export and pilot plan, (2) run cost sim for three prefetch scenarios and share results, (3) provide SOC2 + Private checklist. CinderBridge will share session logs and heatmap, confirm egress constraints, and approve pilot window.
[28:22] Alexei: Sounds good. We'll target the week of Mar 9 for the pilot.
[28:27] Priya: We'll get logs by Mar 2.
[28:29] Tom: I'll double-check firewall rules and KMS policies by Mar 5.
[28:34] Maya: Great, I'll follow up with calendar invite and the links.
[28:38] -- End meeting --

Notes on transcription: There were a few mis-heard words around minute 9 and 26 where numbers were corrected; speaker labels occasionally used "Speaker 1" during screen share.
